text_blocks.snippet: According to guidelines from the American Heart Association and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, high blood pressure (hypertension) starts when your readings are consistently at or above 130/80 mm Hg.

snippet_links.text: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

snippet_highlighted_words: consistently at or above 130/80 mm Hg

text_blocks.snippet: Blood pressure is measured using two numbers: systolic (the top number, measuring pressure when the heart beats) and diastolic (the bottom number, measuring pressure when the heart rests between beats).

list.snippet: Normal: Less than 120 mm Hg systolic and less than 80 mm Hg diastolic
Elevated: 120–129 mm Hg systolic and less than 80 mm Hg diastolic
Stage 1 Hypertension: 130–139 mm Hg systolic or 80–89 mm Hg diastolic
Stage 2 Hypertension: 140 mm Hg or higher systolic or 90 mm Hg or higher diastolic
Severe Hypertension / Hypertensive Crisis: Higher than 180 mm Hg systolic and/or higher than 120 mm Hg diastolic
Elevated: Not yet high blood pressure, but a warning sign to adopt heart-healthy habits to prevent hypertension.
Stage 1: Doctors typically recommend lifestyle changes and may consider medication based on your overall heart disease or stroke risk.
Stage 2: Usually treated with a combination of lifestyle changes and blood pressure medication.

Severe / Crisis: If readings exceed 180/120 mm Hg, rest for five minutes and retest. If it remains that high and you have symptoms like chest pain, shortness of breath, back pain, numbness, or vision changes, call 911 immediately (hypertensive emergency). If you have no symptoms, contact your healthcare provider right away.
